arXiv:2502.08948v2 [math.CO] 13 Jun 2025

Preservation of log-concavity
on gamma polynomials

Luis Ferroni, Greta Panova, and Lorenzo Venturello Address: (L. Ferroni) Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton (NJ), United States
University of Pisa, Pisa, Italy. Email address: ferroni@ias.edu Email address: luis.ferroni@unipi.it Address: (G. Panova) University of Southern California, Los Angeles (CA), United States Email address: gpanova@usc.edu Address: (L. Venturello) Università di Siena, Siena, Italy Email address: lorenzo.venturello@unisi.it
Abstract.

Every symmetric polynomial h⁡(x)h(x) with center of symmetry n/2n/2 can be expressed as a linear combination in the basis xi​(1+x)n−2​ix^{i}(1+x)^{n-2i}. The γ\gamma-polynomial of h⁡(x)h(x), which we denote γh​(x)\gamma_{h}(x), records the coefficients of this linear combination. Two decades ago, Brändén and Gal independently showed that if γh​(x)\gamma_{h}(x) has nonpositive real roots only, then so does h⁡(x)h(x). More recently, Brändén, Ferroni, and Jochemko proved using Lorentzian polynomials that if γh​(x)\gamma_{h}(x) is ultra log-concave, then so is h⁡(x)h(x), and they raised the question of whether a similar statement can be proved for the usual notion of log-concavity. The purpose of this article is to show that the answer to the question of Brändén, Ferroni, and Jochemko is affirmative. One of the crucial ingredients of the proof is an inequality involving binomial numbers that we establish via a path-counting argument.

Key words and phrases:
Log-concave polynomials, γ\gamma-positivity, binomial identities
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A15, 05A19, 05A20

1. Introduction

A recurring endeavor in combinatorics consists in proving that special polynomials satisfy the properties of being unimodal or log-concave. Precisely, a polynomial h⁡(x):=h0+h1​x+⋯+hn​xnh(x):=h_{0}+h_{1}\,x+\cdots+h_{n}\,x^{n} with nonnegative coefficients is said to be unimodal if there exists some index ii such that

h0≤⋯≤hi−1≤hi≥hi+1≥⋯≥hn,h_{0}\leq\cdots\leq h_{i-1}\leq h_{i}\geq h_{i+1}\geq\cdots\geq h_{n},

whereas it is said to be log-concave if, for each 0<i<n0<i<n, the inequalities hi2≥hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}\geq h_{i-1}\,h_{i+1} hold true. If the sequence h0,…,hnh_{0},\ldots,h_{n} has no internal zeros, i.e., if hi​hj≠0h_{i}h_{j}\neq 0 for i<ji<j implies that hk≠0h_{k}\neq 0 for i≤k≤ji\leq k\leq j, then the property of being log-concave implies that of being unimodal. For detailed surveys on unimodality and log-concavity, we refer to [Sta89, Bre94, Brä15].

If the polynomial h⁡(x)h(x) satisfies the conditions hi=hn−ih_{i}=h_{n-i} for each ii, then we say that hh is symmetric with center of symmetry n/2n/2. We note that no assumptions on the degree of h⁡(x)h(x) have been made, thus in particular one is allowed to have hn=0h_{n}=0. Also, notice that the center of symmetry of a symmetric polynomial is unique.

An important tool to prove that such a symmetric polynomial is unimodal consists of proving that it is γ\gamma-positive. Precisely, symmetric polynomials with center of symmetry n/2n/2 can be rewritten as follows:

h⁡(x)=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋γi​xi​(1+x)n−2​i,h(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\gamma_{i}\,x^{i}(1+x)^{n-2i},

where γ0,…​γ⌊n/2⌋\gamma_{0},\ldots\gamma_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} are uniquely determined. Whenever all the coefficients γi\gamma_{i} are nonnegative, then h⁡(x)h(x) is said to be γ\gamma-positive. The γ\gamma-polynomial associated to h⁡(x)h(x) is defined by γh​(x):=γ0+γ1​x+⋯+γ⌊n/2⌋​x⌊n/2⌋\gamma_{h}(x):=\gamma_{0}+\gamma_{1}x+\cdots+\gamma_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}x^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}. It is not difficult to show that γ\gamma-positivity implies unimodality. For a thorough exposition on γ\gamma-positivity, we refer the reader to [Ath18].

Two decades ago, Brändén [Brä06] and Gal [Gal05] showed independently the following result.

Theorem 1.1 ([Brä06, Gal05])

Let h⁡(x)h(x) be a symmetric polynomial. The polynomial γh​(x)\gamma_{h}(x) has only nonpositive real zeros if and only if so does h⁡(x)h(x).

The proof of the above result resorts to basic manipulations of (complex) univariate polynomials. This has been used extensively throughout the literature to approach various problems on unimodality, log-concavity, and real-rootedness.

More recently, Brändén, Ferroni, and Jochemko [BFJ24, Theorem 3.3] proved a version of the above statement, for ultra log-concavity instead. Specifically, the polynomial h⁡(x)=h0+⋯+hn​xnh(x)=h_{0}+\cdots+h_{n}\,x^{n} is said to be ultra log-concave of order m≥nm\geq n if the sequence

h0(m0),h1(m1),…,hn(mn)\frac{h_{0}}{\binom{m}{0}},\frac{h_{1}}{\binom{m}{1}},\ldots,\frac{h_{n}}{\binom{m}{n}}

is log-concave. Their result can be reformulated as follows.

Theorem 1.2 ([BFJ24])

Let h⁡(x)h(x) be a symmetric polynomial with center of symmetry n/2n/2. If γh​(x)\gamma_{h}(x) is ultra log-concave of order ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor with no internal zeros, then h⁡(x)h(x) is ultra log-concave of order nn with no internal zeros.

In contrast to Theorem 1.1, in the last theorem the converse is false, see [BFJ24, Example 3.4]. The proof of Theorem 1.2 relies on properties of the class of Lorentzian polynomials introduced by Brändén and Huh [BH20]. A question raised by Brändén, Ferroni, and Jochemko in their work is whether it was possible to prove a similar property but for the weaker notion of log-concavity. We show that the answer to their question is affirmative. The main result of this article is the following.

Theorem 1.3

Let h⁡(x)h(x) be a symmetric polynomial. If γh​(x)\gamma_{h}(x) is log-concave and has no internal zeros, then h⁡(x)h(x) is log-concave and has no internal zeros.

Once again, and via the same example of Brändén, Ferroni, and Jochemko [BFJ24, Example 3.4], the converse is not true.

A reformulation of Theorem 1.2 is that the operator on bivariate homogeneous polynomials appearing in [BFJ24, Lemma 3.2] preserves the Lorentzian property. Lorentzian polynomials generalize the notion of ultra log-concavity whilst denormalized Lorentzian polynomials generalize the notion of log-concavity. In particular, Theorem 1.3 says that the aforementioned operator preserves the denormalized Lorentzian property too. As it is the case in the present situation, proving the preservation of the denormalized Lorentzian property is often considerably harder. One reason is that Lorentzian polynomials satisfy much better properties than denormalized Lorentzian—for example, nonnegative linear changes of variables preserve the Lorentzian property but often fail to preserve the denormalized Lorentzian property (see [BH20, Theorem 2.10] and [BFJ24, Section 6]). In particular, in order to prove a result like Theorem 1.3, some ad-hoc strategy needs to be applied. In the present article, the proof of Theorem 1.3 is essentially elementary, but relies on certain technical combinatorial identities and inequalities involving binomial coefficients and injections on lattice paths (see Lemma 3.3 and Theorem 4.3).

2. The set up

Throughout the paper a symmetric polynomial h⁡(x)=h0+h1​x+⋯+hn​xnh(x)=h_{0}+h_{1}\,x+\cdots+h_{n}\,x^{n} with center of symmetry n/2n/2 is given. As mentioned earlier, we do not require hn≠0h_{n}\neq 0, so that the degree of h⁡(x)h(x) is allowed to be less than nn. Correspondingly, we will denote γh​(x)=γ0+γ1​x+⋯+γ⌊n/2⌋​x⌊n/2⌋\gamma_{h}(x)=\gamma_{0}+\gamma_{1}\,x+\cdots+\gamma_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\,x^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} the γ\gamma-polynomial associated to h⁡(x)h(x).

The identity h⁡(x)=∑j=0⌊n/2⌋γj​xj​(1+x)n−2​jh(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\gamma_{j}\,x^{j}(1+x)^{n-2j} allows us to establish a relation between the hih_{i}’s in terms of the γj\gamma_{j}’s. More precisely, we have:

(2.1) hi=∑j=0i(n−2​ji−j)​γj,h_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{i}\binom{n-2j}{i-j}\gamma_{j},

for each 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n. Each quantity hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} for 0<i<n0<i<n can be regarded as a homogeneous polynomial of degree 22 in the γj\gamma_{j}’s. However, when written in the basis given by monomials in the γj\gamma_{j}’s, this homogeneous polynomial may have negative coefficients. For concreteness, we include the following example.

Consider n=6n=6, so that h⁡(x)=h0+h1​x+⋯+h6​x6h(x)=h_{0}+h_{1}\,x+\cdots+h_{6}\,x^{6} and, correspondingly, γh​(x)=γ0+γ1​x+γ2​x2+γ3​x3\gamma_{h}(x)=\gamma_{0}+\gamma_{1}\,x+\gamma_{2}\,x^{2}+\gamma_{3}\,x^{3}. We have the following identities:

h0=h6\displaystyle h_{0}=h_{6} =γ0,\displaystyle=\gamma_{0},
h1=h5\displaystyle h_{1}=h_{5} =6​γ0+γ1,\displaystyle=6\,\gamma_{0}+\gamma_{1},
h2=h4\displaystyle h_{2}=h_{4} =15​γ0+4​γ1+γ2,\displaystyle=15\,\gamma_{0}+4\,\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2},

From this, one may compute explicitly:

h12−h0​h2\displaystyle h_{1}^{2}-h_{0}h_{2} =21​γ02+8​γ0​γ1+γ12−γ0​γ2,\displaystyle=21\,\gamma_{0}^{2}+8\,\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{1}^{2}-\gamma_{0}\gamma_{2},

12​γ1​γ3+4​γ2​γ3+γ32,\displaystyle\qquad 12\,\gamma_{1}\gamma_{3}+4\,\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}+\gamma_{3}^{2},

and symmetrically, h42−h3​h5=h22−h1​h3h_{4}^{2}-h_{3}h_{5}=h_{2}^{2}-h_{1}h_{3} and h52−h6​h4=h12−h0​h2h_{5}^{2}-h_{6}h_{4}=h_{1}^{2}-h_{0}h_{2}. Observe the presence of negative signs in the first and the second expression above.

The following is an elementary but important lemma that we will use throughout the proof.

Lemma 2.2

Let a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} be a sequence of nonnegative numbers without internal zeros. The sequence a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} is log-concave if and only if ai​aj−1≥ai−1​aja_{i}a_{j-1}\geq a_{i-1}a_{j} for all 1≤i≤j≤n1\leq i\leq j\leq n.

Proof.

The inequalities ai2≥ai−1​ai+1a_{i}^{2}\geq a_{i-1}a_{i+1} are equivalent to: aiai−1≥ai+1ai\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-1}}\geq\frac{a_{i+1}}{a_{i}}. In other words, the log-concavity of the sequence a0,…,ana_{0},\ldots,a_{n} is equivalent to the sequence b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n}, where bi:=aiai−1b_{i}:=\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-1}}, being weakly decreasing. That is to say that bi≥bjb_{i}\geq b_{j} for i≤ji\leq j which, in terms of the original sequence, reads aiai−1≥ajaj−1\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-1}}\geq\frac{a_{j}}{a_{j-1}} for all i≤ji\leq j. The result follows clearing denominators. ∎

=1176​γ02+700​γ0​γ1+[105​(γ12−γ0​γ2)+315​γ0​γ2]\displaystyle=1176\,\gamma_{0}^{2}+700\,\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}+\left[105\,(\gamma_{1}^{2}-\gamma_{0}\gamma_{2})+315\,\gamma_{0}\gamma_{2}\right]
+[64​(γ1​γ2−γ0​γ3)+120​γ0​γ3]+[10​(γ22−γ1​γ3)+28​(γ1​γ3−γ0​γ4)]\displaystyle\qquad+\left[64\,(\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}-\gamma_{0}\gamma_{3})+120\,\gamma_{0}\gamma_{3}\right]+\left[10\,(\gamma_{2}^{2}-\gamma_{1}\gamma_{3})+28\,(\gamma_{1}\gamma_{3}-\gamma_{0}\gamma_{4})\right]
+[6​(γ2​γ3−γ1​γ4)]+[γ32−γ2​γ4].\displaystyle\qquad+\left[6\,(\gamma_{2}\gamma_{3}-\gamma_{1}\gamma_{4})\right]+\left[\gamma_{3}^{2}-\gamma_{2}\gamma_{4}\right].

By Lemma 2.2, if the sequence γ0,γ1,γ2,γ3,γ4\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4} is log-concave without internal zeros, then all the terms in the last expansion are nonnegative.

The last example helps us outline the idea of the main proof. Notice that inside each of the square brackets all the terms γj​γk\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k} appearing (with either positive or negative sign) have fixed sum j+kj+k. It is tempting to conjecture that hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} will in fact always be a nonnegative combination of terms of the form γj​γk−γj′​γk′\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}-\gamma_{j^{\prime}}\gamma_{k^{\prime}} where j+k=j′+k′j+k=j^{\prime}+k^{\prime} and |j−k|<|j′−k′||j-k|<|j^{\prime}-k^{\prime}|. This is what we will prove in the next sections.

3. The first step of the proof

In general, it is possible to describe the coefficient of each monomial γj​γk\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k} in hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} explicitly. From now on, we define

cj​k(i):=[γj​γk]​(hi2−hi−1​hi+1)c_{jk}^{(i)}:=[\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}]\left(h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1}\right)

where, as customary in combinatorics, the square brackets mean that we extract the coefficient of γj​γk\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k} in the expression hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} regarded as a polynomial in the γj\gamma_{j}’s. In other words:

hi2−hi−1​hi+1=∑j≤kcj​k(i)​γj​γk.h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1}=\sum_{j\leq k}c^{(i)}_{jk}\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}.

It is immediate from (2.1) that cj​k(i)=0c^{(i)}_{jk}=0 whenever k>i+1k>i+1. In other words, the nonvanishing monomials in hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} involve the variables γ0,…,γi+1\gamma_{0},\ldots,\gamma_{i+1} only.

Lemma 3.1

The coefficients cj​k(i)c_{jk}^{(i)} can be computed explicitly as follows:

cj​k(i)={(n−2​ji−j)2−(n−2​ji−j−1)​(n−2​ji−j+1) if j=k,2​(n−2​ji−j)​(n−2​ki−k)−(n−2​ji−j−1)​(n−2​ki−k+1)−(n−2​ji−j+1)​(n−2​ki−k−1) if j<k.c_{jk}^{(i)}=\begin{cases}\binom{n-2j}{i-j}^{2}-\binom{n-2j}{i-j-1}\binom{n-2j}{i-j+1}&\text{ if $j=k$},\\ 2\binom{n-2j}{i-j}\binom{n-2k}{i-k}-\binom{n-2j}{i-j-1}\binom{n-2k}{i-k+1}-\binom{n-2j}{i-j+1}\binom{n-2k}{i-k-1}&\text{ if $j<k$}.\end{cases}
Proof.

The statement follows from (2.1). Indeed, if j<kj<k we have that

[γj​γk]​hi2=2​([γj]​hi)​([γk]​hi)=2​(n−2​ji−j)​(n−2​ki−k),[\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}]h_{i}^{2}=2([\gamma_{j}]h_{i})([\gamma_{k}]h_{i})=2\binom{n-2j}{i-j}\binom{n-2k}{i-k},

and

[γj​γk]​hi−1​hi+1\displaystyle[\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k}]h_{i-1}h_{i+1} =([γj]​hi−1)​([γk]​hi+1)+([γk]​hi−1)​([γj]​hi+1)\displaystyle=([\gamma_{j}]h_{i-1})([\gamma_{k}]h_{i+1})+([\gamma_{k}]h_{i-1})([\gamma_{j}]h_{i+1})
=(n−2​ji−j−1)​(n−2​ki−k+1)+(n−2​ji−j+1)​(n−2​ki−k−1).\displaystyle=\binom{n-2j}{i-j-1}\binom{n-2k}{i-k+1}+\binom{n-2j}{i-j+1}\binom{n-2k}{i-k-1}.

If j=kj=k we have a slightly different expression:

[γj2]​hi2=([γj]​hi)2=(n−2​ji−j)2,[\gamma_{j}^{2}]h_{i}^{2}=([\gamma_{j}]h_{i})^{2}=\binom{n-2j}{i-j}^{2},

and

[γj2]​hi−1​hi+1=([γj]​hi−1)​([γj]​hi+1)=(n−2​ji−j−1)​(n−2​ji−j+1).∎[\gamma_{j}^{2}]h_{i-1}h_{i+1}=([\gamma_{j}]h_{i-1})([\gamma_{j}]h_{i+1})=\binom{n-2j}{i-j-1}\binom{n-2j}{i-j+1}.\qed
Remark 3.2

It is easy to see that the sequence ai=(n−2​ji−j)a_{i}=\binom{n-2j}{i-j} is log-concave for any j≤⌊n/2⌋j\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor. In particular we have that

cj​j(i)=(n−2​ji−j)2−(n−2​ji−j−1)​(n−2​ji−j+1)=ai2−ai−1​ai+1≥0.c^{(i)}_{jj}=\binom{n-2j}{i-j}^{2}-\binom{n-2j}{i-j-1}\binom{n-2j}{i-j+1}=a_{i}^{2}-a_{i-1}a_{i+1}\geq 0.

Moreover, using twice the identity (n−2​jk)=(n−2​(j+1)k)+2​(n−2​(j+1)k−1)+(n−2​(j+1)k−2)\binom{n-2j}{k}=\binom{n-2(j+1)}{k}+2\binom{n-2(j+1)}{k-1}+\binom{n-2(j+1)}{k-2} and letting ai=(n−2​(j+1)i−j)a_{i}=\binom{n-2(j+1)}{i-j} we obtain

cj,j+1(i)\displaystyle c^{(i)}_{j,j+1} =(ai−1​ai−ai−2​ai+1)+4​(ai−12−ai−2​ai)+(ai−2​ai−1−ai−3​ai)≥0,\displaystyle=(a_{i-1}a_{i}-a_{i-2}a_{i+1})+4(a_{i-1}^{2}-a_{i-2}a_{i})+(a_{i-2}a_{i-1}-a_{i-3}a_{i})\geq 0,

where the last inequality follows from the log-concavity of the sequence aia_{i} and Lemma 2.2.

It seems hard to characterize when a coefficient cj​k(i)c_{jk}^{(i)} is negative. However, we prove Lemma 3.3 which describes a structure in the signs of such coefficients, provided that one makes special choices for the parameters. Fix some ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0. We will show that among the coefficients cj​k(i)c_{jk}^{(i)} with j+k=2​ℓj+k=2\ell or j+k=2​ℓ−1j+k=2\ell-1, nonpositive ones can occur only at the “tail”. More precisely, writing such coefficients as a sequence (cℓ,ℓ(i),cℓ−1,ℓ+1(i),cℓ−2,ℓ+2(i),…)(c_{\ell,\ell}^{(i)},c_{\ell-1,\ell+1}^{(i)},c_{\ell-2,\ell+2}^{(i)},\dots) — or similarly (cℓ−1,ℓ(i),cℓ−2,ℓ+1(i),cℓ−3,ℓ+2(i),…)(c_{\ell-1,\ell}^{(i)},c_{\ell-2,\ell+1}^{(i)},c_{\ell-3,\ell+2}^{(i)},\dots) — we show that if this sequence contains a negative number, then all the ones following it must be nonpositive.

Lemma 3.3

Let n≥1n\geq 1, 0≤i≤n/20\leq i\leq n/2 and 1≤ℓ≤(i+1)/21\leq\ell\leq(i+1)/2. Then:

  1. (1)

    If cℓ−j0,ℓ+j0(i)<0c_{\ell-j_{0},\ell+j_{0}}^{(i)}<0, then cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)≤0c_{\ell-j,\ell+j}^{(i)}\leq 0 for every j≥j0j\geq j_{0}.

  2. (2)

    If cℓ−1−j0,ℓ+j0(i)<0c_{\ell-1-j_{0},\ell+j_{0}}^{(i)}<0, then cℓ−1−j,ℓ+j(i)≤0c_{\ell-1-j,\ell+j}^{(i)}\leq 0 for every j≥j0j\geq j_{0}.

Proof.

Let us write the proof for the first of the two sequences in detail, as the other is very similar. What we want to prove is equivalent to showing that for fixed nn, ii, ℓ\ell as in the statement, the sequence {cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)}j=1ℓ\{c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j}\}_{j=1}^{\ell} can possibly become nonpositive only for sufficiently large values of jj.

By Lemma 3.1, for j>0j>0,

(3.1) cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)\displaystyle c_{\ell-j,\ell+j}^{(i)} =2⋅(n−2​ℓ+2​ji−ℓ+j)​(n−2​ℓ−2​ji−ℓ−j)−(n−2​ℓ+2​ji−ℓ+j−1)​(n−2​ℓ−2​ji−ℓ−j+1)−(n−2​ℓ+2​ji−ℓ+j+1)​(n−2​ℓ−2​ji−ℓ−j−1)\displaystyle=2\cdot\tbinom{n-2\ell+2j}{i-\ell+j}\tbinom{n-2\ell-2j}{i-\ell-j}-\tbinom{n-2\ell+2j}{i-\ell+j-1}\tbinom{n-2\ell-2j}{i-\ell-j+1}-\tbinom{n-2\ell+2j}{i-\ell+j+1}\tbinom{n-2\ell-2j}{i-\ell-j-1}
=(n−2​ℓ+2​ji−ℓ+j)​(n−2​ℓ−2​ji−ℓ−j)⋅(2−(i−ℓ+j)​(n−ℓ−j−i)(n−ℓ+j−i+1)​(i−ℓ−j+1)−(i−ℓ−j)​(n−ℓ+j−i)(i−ℓ+j+1)​(n−ℓ−j−i+1))\displaystyle=\tbinom{n-2\ell+2j}{i-\ell+j}\tbinom{n-2\ell-2j}{i-\ell-j}\cdot\left(2-\tfrac{(i-\ell+j)(n-\ell-j-i)}{(n-\ell+j-i+1)(i-\ell-j+1)}-\tfrac{(i-\ell-j)(n-\ell+j-i)}{(i-\ell+j+1)(n-\ell-j-i+1)}\right)
(3.2) =(n−2​ℓ+2​ji−ℓ+j)​(n−2​ℓ−2​ji−ℓ−j)⋅A​j2+B(n−ℓ+j−i+1)​(i−ℓ−j+1)​(i−ℓ+j+1)​(n−ℓ−j−i+1),\displaystyle=\tbinom{n-2\ell+2j}{i-\ell+j}\tbinom{n-2\ell-2j}{i-\ell-j}\cdot\tfrac{Aj^{2}+B}{(n-\ell+j-i+1)(i-\ell-j+1)(i-\ell+j+1)(n-\ell-j-i+1)},

where AA and BB do not depend on jj and are given by:

A\displaystyle A :=−4​n2+16​n​i−16​i2−2​n+4​ℓ−2,\displaystyle:=-4n^{2}+16ni-16i^{2}-2n+4\ell-2,

We are interested in analyzing the sign of cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j} when j≥1j\geq 1. The crucial observation is that the behavior of this sign in the non-trivial cases is dictated only by A​j2+BAj^{2}+B. Sometimes it can vanish, but precisely in those cases we already know what the sign of cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j} is. More precisely, taking, e.g., the term i−ℓ−j+1i-\ell-j+1 appearing in the denominator of (3.2), we may safely assume that it is strictly positive, because if we had ℓ+j>i+1\ell+j>i+1, then the number cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j} is actually zero, and similarly, if ℓ+j=i+1\ell+j=i+1, then cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)<0c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j}<0.

A=−4​(n−2​i)2−2​(n−2​ℓ)−2A=-4(n-2i)^{2}-2(n-2\ell)-2

and each summand is indeed negative. To see the sign of BB, it suffices to replace j=0j=0 in the expression for cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)c_{\ell-j,\ell+j}^{(i)} appearing in (3.1)—an important caveat, however, is that plugging j=0j=0 will not give us cℓ,ℓ(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell,\ell} because the case in which the two lower indices are equal is handled differently by Lemma 3.1. Nonetheless, after taking j=0j=0 in that equation, the resulting value is:

2​((n−2​ℓi−ℓ)2−(n−2​ℓi−ℓ−1)​(n−2​ℓi−ℓ+1)),2\left(\binom{n-2\ell}{i-\ell}^{2}-\binom{n-2\ell}{i-\ell-1}\binom{n-2\ell}{i-\ell+1}\right),

From all the above discussion, we have that the sign of cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j} is given by that A​j2+BAj^{2}+B, and this expression is a quadratic having negative leading term, and evaluates to something nonnegative when j=0j=0. Geometrically, this says that the graph of the function j↦A​j2+Bj\mapsto Aj^{2}+B is a parabola that crosses the jj-axis in exactly one positive value j0j_{0} of jj. In turn, this implies that cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j} will possibly become nonpositive for large jj within the valid range, and from a certain point on. ∎

4. The second step of the proof

Lemma 4.1

Let a0,…,asa_{0},\ldots,a_{s} be a sequence of numbers such that if aj0<0a_{j_{0}}<0 for some index j0j_{0}, then aj≤0a_{j}\leq 0 for all j≥j0j\geq j_{0}. Let b0≥⋯≥bs≥0b_{0}\geq\cdots\geq b_{s}\geq 0 be a weakly decreasing sequence of nonnegative numbers. Then

∑j=0saj≥0⟹∑j=0saj​bj≥0.\sum_{j=0}^{s}a_{j}\geq 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\sum_{j=0}^{s}a_{j}b_{j}\geq 0.
Proof.

Let Ai:=a0+⋯+aiA_{i}:=a_{0}+\cdots+a_{i} for i=0,…,si=0,\ldots,s and set A−1:=0A_{-1}:=0, As+1:=0A_{s+1}:=0, bs+1:=0b_{s+1}:=0. We have that ai>0a_{i}>0 if and only if Ai>Ai−1A_{i}>A_{i-1}, so if j0j_{0} is the first index for which aj0<0a_{j_{0}}<0, then 0≤A0≤A1≤⋯≤Aj0−1>Aj0≥⋯≥As≥00\leq A_{0}\leq A_{1}\leq\cdots\leq A_{j_{0}-1}>A_{j_{0}}\geq\cdots\geq A_{s}\geq 0 and thus {Ai}\{A_{i}\} is a unimodal sequence.

Finally, observe that the following identity holds:

∑i=1sai​bi=∑i=0s(Ai−Ai−1)​bi=∑i=0sAi​(bi−bi+1).\sum_{i=1}^{s}a_{i}b_{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{s}(A_{i}-A_{i-1})b_{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{s}A_{i}(b_{i}-b_{i+1}).

Since each term on the right hand side is nonnegative, the inequality follows. ∎

The last lemma may be applied in the situation of Lemma 3.3. Taking aj=cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)a_{j}=c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j} for each jj, the condition on the signs is satisfied. Taking bj=γℓ−j​γℓ+jb_{j}=\gamma_{\ell-j}\gamma_{\ell+j} for each jj gives a weakly decreasing sequence, thanks to Lemma 2.2. In particular, we have that

∑j≥0cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)≥0⟹∑j≥0cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i)​γℓ−j​γℓ+j≥0.\sum_{j\geq 0}c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j}\geq 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\sum_{j\geq 0}c^{(i)}_{\ell-j,\ell+j}\gamma_{\ell-j}\gamma_{\ell+j}\geq 0.

The condition on the right hand side of the above display is exactly what we need to prove in order to conclude that in hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} the contribution of all the products γj​γk\gamma_{j}\gamma_{k} with fixed j+k=2​ℓj+k=2\ell is nonnegative. An analogous reasoning applies to the case of cℓ−1−j,ℓ+j(i)c^{(i)}_{\ell-1-j,\ell+j}. In summary, we have reduced the problem to showing that the sum on the left and, similarly, the odd counterpart ∑j≥0cℓ−1−j,ℓ+j\sum_{j\geq 0}c_{\ell-1-j,\ell+j}, are nonnegative.

Our next goal is to show that, indeed, the two sums

(4.1) ∑j≥0cℓ−j,ℓ+j(i) and ∑j≥0cℓ−1−j,ℓ+j(i)\sum_{j\geq 0}c_{\ell-j,\ell+j}^{(i)}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\sum_{j\geq 0}c_{\ell-1-j,\ell+j}^{(i)}

are nonnegative. These nonnegativity properties are equivalent to proving the following neat statement, which we will show in the next subsection.

Theorem 4.2

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and let uu be a formal variable, and let γh​(x)=∑j=0⌊n/2⌋uj​xj\gamma_{h}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}u^{j}x^{j}. Then

[ur]​(hi2−hi−1​hi+1)≥0,[u^{r}](h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1})\geq 0,

for every 1≤i≤⌊n2⌋1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor and every r≥0r\geq 0.

The equivalence is immediate, as we are replacing each γk\gamma_{k} by uku^{k}, so that for each index jj we have that γℓ−j​γℓ+j=u2​ℓ\gamma_{\ell-j}\gamma_{\ell+j}=u^{2\ell}, and hence the coefficient of u2​ℓu^{2\ell} in hi2−hi−1​hi+1h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1} is precisely the sum appearing on the left in (4.1) and, similarly, the coefficient of u2​ℓ−1u^{2\ell-1} is the sum on the right. In other words, in light of all the preceding discussion, if we show Theorem 4.2, the proof of Theorem 1.3 follows.

The proof of Theorem 4.2 via lattice paths

This subsection is devoted to the proof of Theorem 4.2. Even though the statement is very simple, the proof we have been able to produce resorts to the enumeration of a complicated family of lattice paths.

First, we make the inequalities to prove more explicit. We have that

h⁡(x,u)=∑j=0⌊n/2⌋uj​xj​(1+x)n−2​j=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋xi​∑j=0i(n−2​ji−j)​uj.h(x;u)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}u^{j}x^{j}(1+x)^{n-2j}=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}x^{i}\sum_{j=0}^{i}\binom{n-2j}{i-j}u^{j}.

Thus,

hi2−hi−1​hi+1=∑j,k=0i(n−2​ji−j)​(n−2​ki−k)​uj+k−∑j,k=0i+1(n−2​ji−1−j)​(n−2​ki+1−k)​uj+k.\displaystyle h_{i}^{2}-h_{i-1}h_{i+1}=\sum_{j,k=0}^{i}\binom{n-2j}{i-j}\binom{n-2k}{i-k}u^{j+k}-\sum_{j,k=0}^{i+1}\binom{n-2j}{i-1-j}\binom{n-2k}{i+1-k}u^{j+k}.

We now show that this quantity is nonnegative.

Theorem 4.3

Let n≥0n\geq 0 and let i≤⌊n2⌋i\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor. Then

(4.2) ∑j,k=0j+k=ri(n−2​ji−j)​(n−2​ki−k)≥∑j,k=0j+k=ri+1(n−2​ji−1−j)​(n−2​ki+1−k),\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,k=0\\ j+k=r\end{subarray}}^{i}\binom{n-2j}{i-j}\binom{n-2k}{i-k}\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,k=0\\ j+k=r\end{subarray}}^{i+1}\binom{n-2j}{i-1-j}\binom{n-2k}{i+1-k},

for every r≥0r\geq 0.

Proof.

We employ a path-counting argument coupled with an injection. First recall that for integers a≤ca\leq c and b≤db\leq d we have that

#​{paths from (a,b) to (c,d)}=(c+d−(a+b)d−b),\#\{\text{paths from $(a,b)$ to $(c,d)$}\}=\binom{c+d-(a+b)}{d-b},

where a path is meant to be a north-east lattice path, i.e., a lattice path using steps +(1,0)+(1,0) or +(0,1)+(0,1).

Fix now r≥0r\geq 0 and consider the lattice point D=(2​n−2​i−r,2​i−r)D=(2n-2i-r,2i-r). Consider first the left hand side (LHS) in (4.2). Let P=(n−2​i,0)P=(n-2i,0) and Q=(n−i,i)Q=(n-i,i). For a lattice point A=(n−i−j,i−j)∈P​QA=(n-i-j,i-j)\in PQ we observe that

#​{paths from O to A}⋅#​{paths from A to D}=(n−2​ji−j)​(2​n−2​r−(n−2​j)2​i−r−(i−j))=(n−2​ji−j)​(n−2​ki−k),\#\{\text{paths from $O$ to $A$}\}\cdot\#\{\text{paths from $A$ to $D$}\}=\\ \binom{n-2j}{i-j}\binom{2n-2r-(n-2j)}{2i-r-(i-j)}=\binom{n-2j}{i-j}\binom{n-2k}{i-k},

where in the last identity we used that j+k=rj+k=r. In other words, the summands in the LHS of (4.2) are the product of number of paths from OO to AA and from AA to DD as AA varies in the segment P​QPQ. These are the paths contained in the yellow rectangles depicted in Figure 1. By a double counting argument we can compute the LHS also by counting the paths from OO to DD, where each path contributes for the number of lattice points in P​QPQ it intersects. More precisely:

LHS =∑A∈P​Q∩ℤ2#⁡{paths from O to A}​#​{paths from A to D}\displaystyle=\sum_{A\in PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\#\{\text{paths from $O$ to $A$}\}\#\{\text{paths from $A$ to $D$}\}
=∑α​ path from O to D∑A∈α∩P​Q1\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path from $O$ to $D$}}\sum_{A\in\alpha\cap PQ}1
=∑α​ path from O to D#⁡{α∩P​Q}\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path from $O$ to $D$}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}

Now, let us consider the right hand side (RHS) of (4.2). We employ a similar strategy. Let P′=(n−2​i+2,0)P^{\prime}=(n-2i+2,0) and Q′=(n−i+1,i−1)Q^{\prime}=(n-i+1,i-1). For any lattice point A′=(n−i+1−j,i−1−j)∈P′​Q′A^{\prime}=(n-i+1-j,i-1-j)\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime} we have that

#​{paths from O to A′}​#​{paths from A′ to D}=(n−2​ji−1−j)​(2​n−2​r−(n−2​j)2​i−r−(i−1−j))=(n−2​ji−1−j)​(n−2​ki+1−k).\#\{\text{paths from $O$ to $A^{\prime}$}\}\#\{\text{paths from $A^{\prime}$ to $D$}\}=\\ \binom{n-2j}{i-1-j}\binom{2n-2r-(n-2j)}{2i-r-(i-1-j)}=\binom{n-2j}{i-1-j}\binom{n-2k}{i+1-k}.

See Figure 2 for an illustration. In particular,

RHS =∑A′∈P′​Q′∩ℤ2#⁡{paths from O to A′}​#​{paths from A′ to D}\displaystyle=\sum_{A^{\prime}\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}}\#\{\text{paths from $O$ to $A^{\prime}$}\}\#\{\text{paths from $A^{\prime}$ to $D$}\}
=∑α​ path from O to D∑A′∈α∩P′​Q′1\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path from $O$ to $D$}}\sum_{A^{\prime}\in\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}}1
=∑α​ path from O to D#⁡{α∩P′​Q′}.\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path from $O$ to $D$}}\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}.
Claim 4.4

If α\alpha is a path from OO to DD such that α∩P′​Q′≠∅\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\neq\varnothing, then α∩P​Q≠∅\alpha\cap PQ\neq\varnothing.

Proof of Claim 4.4.

Let B′=(x′,y′)∈α∩P′​Q′B^{\prime}=(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}. In particular, x′−y′=n−2​i+2x^{\prime}-y^{\prime}=n-2i+2 and 0≤y′≤i−10\leq y^{\prime}\leq i-1. Walking backwards (from B′B^{\prime} to OO) in α\alpha the difference between the first and second coordinate of a point either increases or decreases by one, and the second coordinate weakly decreases. Since OO is in α\alpha, the difference between the coordinates will eventually be 00. By continuity, there exists a lattice point B=(x,y)∈αB=(x,y)\in\alpha such that x−y=n−2​ix-y=n-2i and 0≤y≤i−10\leq y\leq i-1. So B∈α∩P​QB\in\alpha\cap PQ. ∎

Observe that the natural lattice partial order in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}, which we denote with ≤\leq induces a total order in P​Q∩ℤ2PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2} and P′​Q′∩ℤ2P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}. If α\alpha is a path from OO to DD such that α∩P′​Q′≠∅\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\neq\varnothing we denote by max⁡{α∩P′​Q′}\max\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\} the maximal element with respect to this order. By Claim 4.4 we have that α∩P​Q≠∅\alpha\cap PQ\neq\varnothing, and we denote by min⁡{α∩P​Q}\operatorname{min}\{\alpha\cap PQ\} its minimal element. Since in the proof of Claim 4.4 we showed that given B′∈α∩P′​Q′B^{\prime}\in\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime} there exists B∈α∩P​QB\in\alpha\cap PQ with B≤B′B\leq B^{\prime}, we have that min⁡{α∩P​Q}≤max⁡{α∩P′​Q′}\operatorname{min}\{\alpha\cap PQ\}\leq\max\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}. We will refine the path counting using these elements in the following way: any path α\alpha from OO to DD which intersects P′​Q′P^{\prime}Q^{\prime} can be written uniquely as the concatenation of a path α1\alpha_{1} from OO to min⁡{α∩P​Q}\operatorname{min}\{\alpha\cap PQ\}, a path α2\alpha_{2} from min⁡{α∩P​Q}\operatorname{min}\{\alpha\cap PQ\} to max⁡{α∩P′​Q′}\max\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\} and a path α3\alpha_{3} from max⁡{α∩P′​Q′}\max\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\} to DD. In terms of lattice point count we have that

(4.3) {α∩P​Q}={α2∩P​Q}∪{α3∩P​Q}\{\alpha\cap PQ\}=\{\alpha_{2}\cap PQ\}\cup\{\alpha_{3}\cap PQ\}

and

(4.4) {α∩P′​Q′}={α2∩P′​Q′}.\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}=\{\alpha_{2}\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}.

The next claim shows that the sum of the contributions of the intermediate paths vanishes.

Claim 4.5

Let R∈P​Q∩ℤ2R\in PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2} and R′∈P′​Q′∩ℤ2R^{\prime}\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}, with R≤R′R\leq R^{\prime}. Then

∑α​ path R→R′#⁡{α∩P​Q}=∑α​ path R→R′#⁡{α∩P′​Q′}.\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $R\to R^{\prime}$}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $R\to R^{\prime}$}}\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}.
Proof of Claim 4.5.

The rotation by 180∘180^{\circ} around the barycenter of the rectangle spanned by RR and R′R^{\prime} induces an involution φ\varphi on the set of paths from RR to R′R^{\prime}. Moreover, this map sends lattice points of P​QPQ to lattice points of P′​Q′P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}. See Figure 3 for an illustration of the map φ\varphi, showing how the three lattice points in the intersection of the path on the left with P​QPQ (the blue segment) correspond to three lattice points in the intersection of the path on the right with P′​Q′P^{\prime}Q^{\prime} (the red segment). We obtain

∑α​ path R→R′#⁡{α∩P​Q}\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $R\to R^{\prime}$}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\} =∑α​ path R→R′#⁡{φ⁡(α)∩P​Q}\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $R\to R^{\prime}$}}\#\{\varphi(\alpha)\cap PQ\}
=∑α​ path R→R′#⁡{α∩P′​Q′}.∎\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $R\to R^{\prime}$}}\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}.\qed

Finally, we can show that the difference LHS−RHS\text{LHS}-\text{RHS} is nonnegative:

LHS−RHS\displaystyle\text{LHS}-\text{RHS} =∑α​ path O→D(#⁡{α∩P​Q}−#⁡{α∩P′​Q′})\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}}\left(\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}-\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}\right)
=∑α​ path O→Dα∩P′​Q′=∅#⁡{α∩P​Q}+∑α​ path O→Dα∩P′​Q′≠∅(#⁡{α∩P​Q}−#⁡{α∩P′​Q′})\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\varnothing\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\neq\varnothing\end{subarray}}\left(\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}-\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}\right)
=∑α​ path O→Dα∩P′​Q′=∅#⁡{α∩P​Q}\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\varnothing\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}
+∑R∈P​Q∩ℤ2R′∈P′​Q′∩ℤ2R≤R′(∑α​ path O to Dmin⁡{α∩P​Q}=Rmax⁡{α∩P′​Q′}=R′(#{α∩PQ}−#{α∩P′Q′})).\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\in PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R^{\prime}\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R\leq R^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O$ to $D$}\\ \operatorname{min}\{\alpha\cap PQ\}=R\\ \max\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}=R^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\left(\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}-\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}\right)\right).

We now combine (4.3) and (4.4):

(4.5) LHS−RHS=∑α​ path O→Dα∩P′​Q′=∅#⁡{α∩P​Q}+∑R∈P​Q∩ℤ2R′∈P′​Q′∩ℤ2R≤R′[∑α​ path R to R′(#⁡{α∩P​Q}−#⁡{α∩P′​Q′})+∑α​ path R′ to Dα∩P′​Q′={R′}#⁡{α∩P​Q}]=∑α​ path O→Dα∩P′​Q′=∅#⁡{α∩P​Q}+∑R∈P​Q∩ℤ2R′∈P′​Q′∩ℤ2R≤R′∑α​ path R′ to Dα∩P′​Q′={R′}#⁡{α∩P​Q},\text{LHS}-\text{RHS}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\varnothing\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}\kern 5.0pt+\\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\in PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R^{\prime}\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R\leq R^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\left[\sum_{\alpha\text{ path $R$ to $R^{\prime}$}}\left(\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}-\#\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\}\right)+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $R^{\prime}$ to $D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\{R^{\prime}\}\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}\right]\\ =\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\varnothing\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\in PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R^{\prime}\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R\leq R^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $R^{\prime}$ to $D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\{R^{\prime}\}\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\},

where the last equality follows from Claim 4.5. In particular, LHS−RHS≥0\text{LHS}-\text{RHS}\geq 0. ∎

Example 4.6

Let n=6n=6, i=2i=2 and r=2r=2. By Example 2.1 we know that c1,1(2)+c0,2(2)=28c_{1,1}^{(2)}+c_{0,2}^{(2)}=28 and, by (4.5) in the proof of Theorem 4.3, we know that this number is equal to

∑α​ path O→Dα∩P′​Q′=∅#⁡{α∩P​Q}+∑R∈P​Q∩ℤ2R′∈P′​Q′∩ℤ2R≤R′∑α​ path R′ to Dα∩P′​Q′={R′}#⁡{α∩P​Q},\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $O\to D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\varnothing\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}R\in PQ\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R^{\prime}\in P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}\\ R\leq R^{\prime}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\text{ path $R^{\prime}$ to $D$}\\ \alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}=\{R^{\prime}\}\end{subarray}}\#\{\alpha\cap PQ\},

with D=(6,2)D=(6,2), P=(2,0)P=(2,0), Q=(4,2)Q=(4,2), P′=(4,0)P^{\prime}=(4,0) and Q′=(5,1)Q^{\prime}=(5,1). Figure 4 shows the 15 paths which give a non-trivial contribution to these sums. Fourteen of them do not intersect P′​Q′P^{\prime}Q^{\prime} (the red segment), and each contributes to the first sum with the number of intersections with P​QPQ (the blue segment). The sum of these numbers is 27. One of them, the one in the third row and first column, contributes with a 1 to the second sum: indeed it contains a subpath from R′=P′R^{\prime}=P^{\prime} to DD which intersects P​QPQ. Hence the contributions sum up to 2828.

Remark 4.7

When r≥i+1r\geq i+1 the second coordinate of Q′Q^{\prime} is larger than or equal to the second coordinate of DD. In other words Q′Q^{\prime} is “above” DD. In this case, each path from OO to DD intersects P′​Q′P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}. For the same reason, we have that max⁡{α∩P′​Q′}\max\{\alpha\cap P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}\} is larger than any point in α∩P​Q\alpha\cap PQ, and hence there is no non-zero contribution to the second sum of (4.5). Following the proof of Theorem 4.3 this implies that ∑j,k=0i+j=ricj​k(i)=0\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j,k=0\\ i+j=r\end{subarray}}^{i}{c_{jk}^{(i)}}=0. We observe that there is another way to see this identity when r≥i+1r\geq i+1 using generating functions. Indeed, by [Wil94, Eq. (2.5.15)] we have that

(n−2​ji−j)=(2​(i−j)+(n−2​i)i−j)=[xn−i−j]​(1−1−4​x)n−2​i2​1−4​x,\binom{n-2j}{i-j}=\binom{2(i-j)+(n-2i)}{i-j}=[x^{n-i-j}]\frac{(1-\sqrt{1-4x})^{n-2i}}{2\sqrt{1-4x}},

where the square brackets indicate the coefficient in the power series expansion. When r≥i+1r\geq i+1, both the LHS and the RHS of (4.2) are equal to

[x2​n−2​i−r]​((1−1−4​x)n−2​i2​1−4​x)2.[x^{2n-2i-r}]\left(\frac{(1-\sqrt{1-4x})^{n-2i}}{2\sqrt{1-4x}}\right)^{2}.

Moreover, the computation in (4.5) implies that it is possible to express the difference between both sides in (4.2) as a manifestly positive expression involving binomial coefficients. An alternative approach that performs this computation via the Wilf–Zeilberger method was privately communicated to us by Tewodros Amdeberhan.
